name: Carlos Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a cardboard box plant, on the folder-gluer. Big sheets of printed cardboard come off the printer, and my machine folds them, glues the flap and spits out flat boxes that I stack onto pallets. Mostly pizza boxes and boxes for a supermarket's own-brand cereal. I've been there just over a year and I'm still the one who jams it when we change box sizes, there's a guy called Big Sal who sorts it out in two minutes.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The pay's good for round here, with the shift bonus, and it's ten minutes from my flat on the bike. My grandad left me his flat, so I don't pay rent, which is why I've got a decent bit saved. I like knowing what I'm doing each day. I'm not a big one for change, my girlfriend Marta says I'd eat the same lunch for ten years if she let me, and she's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, all that fuss for nothing. Probably wouldn't post anything, I'm not really online apart from football stuff. At work we'd have a laugh about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's fine by me. I didn't want anything to change anyway. I'd just keep getting better at the folder-gluer and maybe one day I'll be the one who fixes jams in two minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and over the next year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. I'd keep putting about six hundred a month away and keep cycling in. Maybe Marta and I would finally book that trip to the coast we keep talking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing to feel, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe one day you'll fix jams in two minutes. What's stopping you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly I panic and start pulling sheets out, and that makes it worse. Big Sal says you have to stop, look where the board's catching, and adjust the guide. I know that, I just don't do it yet when the alarm's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever use AI tools for anything, at work or at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Marta uses it to write captions for her salon's page, but I don't see what I'd use it for. I've got a phone for messages and football scores and that's enough.

S0.say: I'd say there you go, all that fuss for nothing. He wouldn't post anything, but there'd be a laugh about it at work.
S0.think: It's fine by him because he didn't want change anyway. He'd keep improving on the folder-gluer, hoping to fix jams as fast as Big Sal one day.
S0.do: Carries on as now, saving about six hundred a month and cycling to work. Considers finally booking a coast trip with his girlfriend Marta.
S0.feel: Calm, with nothing much to feel.
S0.quote: I know that, I just don't do it yet when the alarm's going.
S0.fieldNote: His contentment is genuine and simple: rent-free flat, good pay, short commute. He's frank about his skill gap. He has no interest in AI tools and doesn't feel he's missing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's how business goes. Companies always bring in new machines, and people get used to them. I wouldn't make a big thing of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably be fine. There's three or four box plants on the industrial estate and they're always hiring for night shift. If my job changes, I'd learn the new bit slowly, and if they don't want me, I'd go next door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do what the supervisor asks. If they bring in a robot stacker, I'd learn whatever button I have to press. I wouldn't do any course unless they made me, and I wouldn't change jobs unless I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Maybe a little bit annoyed at having to learn new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go next door. Have you looked at what those other plants pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not properly. Sal says the one on the corner pays a bit less but has a better canteen. I'd look if I had to, but I don't like looking for jobs, it feels like going to the dentist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the new jobs that appear are ones you'd need to retrain for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd probably wait and see if I really needed to. Most of the time these things are slower than people say. I've got no rent and some savings, so I'm not in a rush.

S1.say: I'd say that's how business goes: companies bring in new machines and people get used to them. He wouldn't make a big thing of it.
S1.think: He expects to be fine because several box plants nearby hire for nights. He'd learn new bits slowly or move next door if pushed out.
S1.do: Keeps his head down and learns whatever button a new robot stacker needs. Avoids courses unless required and only changes jobs if forced.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, a bit annoyed at having to learn new things.
S1.quote: I don't like looking for jobs, it feels like going to the dentist.
S1.fieldNote: His no-rent flat and nearby plants let him treat steady change as someone else's problem. His centre outlook shows as not blaming anyone. Resistance shows as waiting it out, which his cushion makes affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't know what anyone's supposed to do about that. It's not like anyone's in charge of it. I'd probably just say, crazy times, and change the subject.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and robots can do my job and Sal's job and the job next door. That's the bit that gets me, there's no next door anymore. I don't know how to do anything else, and I'm not quick at learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on extras straight away, no trip, no new bike. I'd hang on to my job until they told me to go, and I'd talk to Marta about whether her salon would last, because people still want a person cutting their hair, I think. I'd probably look into whatever help the government offered, even though I've never claimed anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there's no next door anymore. Is that the worst part for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. My whole plan, if you can call it a plan, was if this goes wrong, I'll go next door. I've never needed a backup to the backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trip to the coast, for sure. Then football on Thursday night, it's twelve a week for the pitch. The flat's paid for, so at least I won't lose that, thank you Grandad.

S2.say: I'd say I don't know what anyone's supposed to do, since nobody's in charge of it. He'd call it crazy times and change the subject.
S2.think: Robots taking his job, Sal's job and the jobs next door in two years removes his only backup plan. He doesn't know how to do anything else and learns slowly.
S2.do: Cuts extras immediately, starting with the coast trip and Thursday football. Holds on to his job until told to go, checks whether Marta's salon would last, and looks into government help for the first time.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep, which is unusual for him.
S2.quote: My whole plan, if you can call it a plan, was if this goes wrong, I'll go next door. I've never needed a backup to the backup.
S2.fieldNote: His calm in the first two pictures rests entirely on 'next door', and when that goes he swings sharply. Publicly he deflects; privately he's shaken. The paid-off flat is his only real anchor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is quick, but people will work something out. Maybe the government does something, maybe the companies do. I'd say I'm not panicking yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means it'll hit the big plants first and the small ones later, so I might get a few years of moving between them. But I'm not good at learning new stuff, so I'd be watching people younger than me get the robot jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and save extra, maybe eight hundred a month instead of six. I'd ask Sal if he thinks I should learn the maintenance side, and if he says yes I might do it, slowly. Mostly I'd wait and see which way it goes before doing anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It'd be on my mind at work, like a noise in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people younger than you would get the robot jobs. You're twenty-seven. Who's younger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair, I'm not old. I mean people who are quick with screens, the lads who come in from college already knowing the software. I'm young but I learn like an old man, Marta says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see before doing anything big. When would you stop waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When they put a robot on my machine, I suppose. That's when it's real. Before that, it's all just talk on the news.

S3.say: I'd say five years is quick but people will work something out, maybe the government or the companies. He'd say he's not panicking yet.
S3.think: He expects big plants to automate first, giving him a few years to move between smaller ones. He fears quicker, screen-savvy newcomers would get the robot jobs.
S3.do: Keeps working and lifts savings from six to eight hundred a month. Asks Sal whether to learn maintenance and might do it slowly, but mostly waits to see which way it goes.
S3.feel: Anxious, like a constant noise in the background at work.
S3.quote: I'm young but I learn like an old man, Marta says.
S3.fieldNote: He would only act once a robot is put on his own machine, which shows how firmly he waits. He sees his slowness with screens as the real handicap, not his age. Extra savings are his main response.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off, anything could happen. Half the stuff they predict never happens. I'd say I'll worry about it when it gets closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels like forever. I'd be thirty-seven. I know I should do something with that time, but I also know I probably wouldn't until year eight or nine, that's just how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first few years I'd carry on like normal and keep saving. Maybe around year five, if it looked real, I'd do a maintenance course, because someone has to fix the robots. I'd keep the flat paid off, which it is, and not take on any loans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not much, but a bit, the kind you push to the back of your head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably not act until year eight or nine. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, when you put it like that. My dad was the same, he knew the warehouse was closing two years before it did and still acted surprised. I don't want to be like that, but I probably am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Marta pushed me, honestly. Or if Sal did a course and said it was easy. I need someone I trust to go first and tell me it's fine.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long way off and half of what's predicted never happens. He'd worry about it when it gets closer.
S4.think: Ten years feels like forever; he knows he should use the time but admits he probably wouldn't act until year eight or nine.
S4.do: Carries on normally and keeps saving for several years. Considers a maintenance course around year five if it looks real, and avoids any loans while keeping his flat debt-free.
S4.feel: A mild unease he pushes to the back of his mind.
S4.quote: My dad was the same, he knew the warehouse was closing two years before it did and still acted surprised.
S4.fieldNote: More time makes him calmer, but mostly through putting it off, and he recognises the pattern from his father. He needs a trusted person like Marta or Sal to go first. His cushion makes delay feel safe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no next door to go to. What would help is someone, the plant or the government, just telling me clearly what to learn and paying me while I learn it. I'm not good at figuring it out alone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe you should have asked about Marta's job. Everyone talks about factories, but if people stop having money, they stop getting haircuts too. We'd both be in trouble at the same time.

headlineQuote: I'm not a big one for change, my girlfriend Marta says I'd eat the same lunch for ten years if she let me, and she's right.
portrait: Carlos Baker is a 27-year-old junior operator on the folder-gluer at a cardboard box plant, still slow to clear jams, living rent-free in the flat his grandfather left him with his girlfriend Marta, a hairdresser. He saves about six hundred a month, never uses AI and dislikes change. With a plateau or steady change he stays calm because there's always another box plant next door. AGI in two years alarms him because that backup disappears. With five or ten years he slides back into waiting, admitting he'd likely put off action as his father did.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no other plant next door to move to.
whatWouldHelp: Someone, either the plant or the government, telling him clearly what to learn and paying him while he learns it.
